# How This Module Works

## What the Module Covers: The Linear Regression Model

The module does one thing thoroughly: the linear regression model.
The term runs from what a sample is to reading a residual plot.

::: {.takeaway title="Run One, and Name Its Assumption"}
You can run a regression and say what its coefficient hides. You can name the
assumption that would license a causal reading.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- 15-32 min. The whole block is capped at seventeen minutes and the cap is

     read aloud concludes the module is low-stakes, and this is the
     best-attended slot of the term. Anything not on these five frames is in
     the appendix or the outline.

     Wooldridge chapter 1, p.1, opens a first course on the same ground:
     what econometrics is for, what kinds of data exist, and why causality
     is hard. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Name what the module does NOT cover as well: no matrix algebra, no panel data,
no panel methods. Those are Part II and they exist because the problem this
module ends on is hard.
:::

## How the Four Blocks Fit Together

- **Foundations:** what a sample is, and why one estimate is only one draw.
- **Simple Regression:** one line, its derivation, and how far to trust it.
- **Multiple Regression:** what holding other things fixed buys, and what omitting them costs.
- **Limits:** what breaks, how you would know, and what regression cannot license.

::: {.takeaway title="Simple Before Multiple Regression"}
Lecture 3.1 is unreadable without 2.1 to 2.4. Block 4 is where the module stops
being mechanical.
:::


::: {.notes}
This is a dependency structure, not a list of weeks. Blocks 2 and 3 are one

Miss the middle of that and the second half of the term is unreadable.

## The Question We Ask Every Week

Regression says how two things vary together. Whether co-movement licenses a
causal claim depends on the design, not the estimator.

::: {.caveat title="The Standing Question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

```{=html}

     Today's instance is at 97 minutes. Announce the ritual here; do not run

```

::: {.notes}
Usually the honest answer is that the design does not license the causal claim.
Say that now, so the room does not read the weekly slot as a formality with a

- **The Derivation:** in the appendix of its deck, and set as homework.

# Populations and Samples

## The Gap Between the Population and the Sample

Two groups of people, and the whole module is the argument between them:

- **Population:** every person the question is about.
- **Sample:** the handful of those people whose numbers we hold.
- **The Whole Module:** an argument from the sample back to the population.

::: {.takeaway title="No Technique Closes the Gap"}
Nothing later in the term removes the gap. Later techniques only say honestly
how wide the gap might be.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- IDEA 1. 32-53 min.

     Wooldridge C-1, p.714: "By population, we mean any well-defined group of
     subjects", and a parameter is a constant of that population. His own
     example is the return to another year of education, which is the
     module's question, so the section and the hook share a source. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Sixty seconds on how a sample goes wrong, if the room is with you. Everyone at
a graduate careers fair, everyone who answers a landline on a Tuesday
afternoon, everyone on LinkedIn: all three are biased, and the useful question
is which way each one tilts earnings. This used to be a question frame; the
answer is obvious enough that it did not earn the room time.

Insist on the word "every". A population is not a big sample; it is the whole
group the answer is a fact about, and the question decides who is in it. Ask
whose earnings are in the population for today's question: everyone in Ireland,
everyone working, everyone who ever worked?
:::

## Notation for a Single Observation

A sample is a list of pairs, one for each person in it:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\left\{ \left( x_i, y_i \right) \right\}_{i=1}^{n}
\end{equation}
```

- $x_i$: years of schooling completed by person $i$
- $y_i$: hourly earnings of person $i$, in euro
- $i$: which person, running from 1 to $n$
- $n$: how many people are in the sample

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-1a, p.714, writes the random sample as {Y_1, ..., Y_n}
     drawn i.i.d. from f(y; theta), and C-2a, p.715, distinguishes the
     random variables from the realised numbers {y_1, ..., y_n}. This deck
     uses lower case throughout because capital X is not introduced until
     2.1; the distinction between the variable and its realisation is 1.3's
     job, not week one's. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Write one row on the board: person 7, twelve years of schooling, 9.80 an hour.
The subscript is an address, not an ordering, and nothing about person 7 makes
them seventh in any meaningful sense.
:::

## Cross-Section, Time Series and Panel Data

What you can estimate depends on how the data is indexed:

- **Cross-Section Data:** many people, each seen once, indexed by $i$.
- **Time-Series Data:** one unit, seen over many periods, indexed by $t$.
- **Panel Data:** many people, each over many periods, indexed by $i$ and $t$.

::: {.takeaway title="Every Dataset Here Is Cross-Section"}
Our 120 people are each observed once. The assumptions change when the
subscript does.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Added 17 September, on Sam's question. Wooldridge chapter 1 opens a

     Lambert has a short video "Time series vs cross sectional data" for
     the Read item.

     THE REASON IT EARNS A FRAME, beyond completeness. Two problems it
     fixes. First, i was being introduced as though it were the only
     subscript there is, which makes the notation look arbitrary rather
     than chosen. Second, and larger: 4.1 has a whole section on SERIAL
     CORRELATION, the t subscript appears nowhere in the module, and the
     orientation section of this deck tells students there is no time
     series. Those three cannot all stand. This frame lets 4.1 say that
     serial correlation is a t-shaped fault and that we meet it in
     i-shaped data because the residual plot looks identical - which is

     SCOPE. Three structures, named by subscript, and nothing else. Pooled
     cross-sections are deliberately absent: a fourth row would be a
     taxonomy, and the module never uses any of them but the first. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Two minutes, no more. The only thing to land is that the subscript is a claim
about what varies, and that everything this term holds $i$ fixed as the thing
that varies.

Flag the one exception rather than leaving it to ambush them in week eleven.
Lecture 4.1 covers serial correlation, which is a fault of $t$-indexed data.
We meet it anyway, in our cross-section, because a mis-specified curve leaves a
residual plot that looks exactly like the time-series version - and being able
to tell those two apart is the point of that lecture rather than a detour.

If anyone asks about panel data, it is Part II, and it is where most modern
applied work lives.
:::

## Roman for What We Know, Greek for What We Want to Know

Roman here means the everyday alphabet, the one English is written in. Our
sample holds $n$ people; the population holds $N$.

::: {.caveat title="Never the Same Number"}
Every summary from here comes as a pair: a Roman letter computed from our 120,
and a Greek letter for the fact about all 200,000 that nobody sees.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge C-1, p.714: a parameter is a constant of the population;
     C-2a, p.715: an estimator is a rule applied to the sample, and changes
     with the sample. The Roman/Greek convention is this module's, not the
     book's, but it encodes exactly that distinction. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Say "Roman" once and then say what it means, because the word is doing three
jobs in a maths context and a student has no reason to pick the right one.
Roman numerals are the obvious wrong guess and they are sitting right there; in
typesetting "roman" means upright rather than italic, which is a second wrong
guess, and our variables are italic anyway. The everyday alphabet is all that
is meant. Thirty seconds spent killing that ambiguity is cheaper than a term of
students half-reading every symbol.

A line of algebra that slides from a Roman letter to a Greek one is the move
this module exists to make you suspicious of. Watch for it in your own working
all term: the moment you write an equals sign between a sample quantity and a
population quantity, you have assumed the thing being estimated.
:::

## Why a Simulated Population Rather Than Real Data

Real earnings data gives an estimate and never says whether it was good. Here
the truth is written down. Every estimate this term can be marked against 1.30.

::: {.defn title="The Flaws Are Already Switched Off"}
Lecture 3.1 turns on an omitted variable and Lecture 4.2 a mismeasured one. Lecture 4.1
turns on an error whose size grows with schooling.
:::

::: {.notes}
Real data arrives with all three switched on at once and no label saying which.
That is the whole difficulty, and it is why the module spends eleven weeks
building the apparatus before Lecture 4.2 asks what the apparatus cannot do.
:::

## The Training Sample and the Hold-Out Sample

The 120 we work with is the **training** sample. A second 120 was drawn at the
same time and put away unopened. The second draw is the **hold-out**, or test,
sample. Statistics and machine learning both call the pair a train-test split
[@james2021].

::: {.takeaway title="A Fit Proves Nothing Alone"}
Anything can be made to fit the data it was chosen on. The only honest check is
data the choice never saw.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- @james2021 is in the .bib and is the standard reference for the split,
     but it is NOT on this module's two-book shelf. Flagged for the shelf
     pass: either put the file in 1-1_Data-and-Variation/references/ or
     drop the citation. -->
```

::: {.notes}
We open the hold-out in Lecture 2.2, once there is a line worth testing. Until then
it stays shut, and that discipline is the whole point of having drawn it. Say
plainly that opening it early is the statistical equivalent of marking your own
exam script.
:::

# Describing One Variable

## The Mean Is Where the Distribution Balances

The mean is the one number that stands in for everybody. It is the point where
deviations above and below sum to zero:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i
\end{equation}
```

- $\sum_{i=1}^{n}$: add up what follows, over all $n$ people in the sample
- $\bar{x}$: said "x-bar", where the bar means the average of $x$
- $\mu_x$: the average of $x$ across the population

```{=html}
<!-- IDEA 2. 56-78 min.

     Wooldridge B-3a, p.691: the expected value is a weighted average of the
     possible values, and "sometimes the expected value is called the
     population mean". That is exactly the gloss on the E[.] line. B-3b,

```

::: {.notes}
Read the sigma out loud before anything else, because it is the first piece of
notation in the module that a weaker student will not already own: "add up
x-sub-i, for i running from one to n". Say that the subscript is an address, not
a power, and that the sign is an instruction rather than a quantity.

Balance is not a metaphor here: the mean is the point where the deviations
above it and below it sum to zero, and that identity is what makes the cross
term in this week's derivation behave.

Our population averages 13.54 years of schooling and 11.52 euro an hour. Both
are facts about the generator, and neither is ever computed from a sample.

E[.] is introduced once, here, and never re-listed. Lecture 1.2 puts something
inside the brackets other than a bare variable.
:::

## Why the Bar Marks a Sample Quantity

A bar over a letter means the average of that letter. Statistics marks sample
averages this way everywhere, not only here. Our 120 earn 12.25 an hour on
average; the population earns 11.52.

::: {.caveat title="Redraw and the Bar Changes"}
$\bar{x}$ is arithmetic you can do this afternoon on 120 numbers. $\mu_x$ is a
fact about 200,000 people that you will never compute. Draw a different 120 and
$\bar{x}$ changes; $\mu_x$ does not.
:::

::: {.notes}
Say it out loud as "x-bar" and make the room say it back, because a symbol
nobody can pronounce is a symbol nobody reads. The mark goes on whatever was
averaged, so y-bar is the average of y. Lecture 1.3 adds the hat, which marks
any sample estimate rather than a mean specifically.

Redraw the 120 and the bar changes while mu does not: that sentence is the
entire content of Lecture 1.3 and it is worth writing down now. Everything the
module does from here is measure how far a Roman letter wanders from the Greek
one it is aimed at.

The 0.73 between 12.25 and 11.52 is the whole subject. Nobody outside this room
ever gets to see it.
:::

## Expectation: The Population Average of an Expression

$\mu_x$ is the population average of $x$ itself. We also want the population
average of things built from $x$:

::: {.defn title="An Operator, Not a Quantity"}
$E[\cdot]$ takes whatever expression sits inside it and returns its population
average. $E[x]$ is $\mu_x$; feed it something else and you get something else.
:::

Lecture 1.2 is about this operator. Today it is only notation.

```{=html}
<!-- Added 17 September. E[.] had been a single notation line on the mean
     frame - "the population average of whatever is inside" - which is a
     gloss, not an explanation, and an operator is a different kind of
     object from the quantities beside it in that list. It also does real
     work three frames on: the central moments frame is one operator fed
     three different powers, and that only reads if the room knows E[.]
     takes an argument.

     Scope is deliberately narrow. This frame teaches the NOTATION; Lecture
     1.2 teaches what an expectation IS - a property of a distribution that
     exists before anyone collects data. The closing line says so, to stop
     the two frames reading as a repeat. Wooldridge B-3a p.691 for the
     expected value and the term "population mean". -->
```

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds, and resist expanding it - next week is the lecture. The point
to land is that the brackets take an argument, because everything in section
two is that one operator fed a different expression: $x$ gives the mean,
$(x - \mu_x)^2$ gives the variance, and the higher powers give the shape.

If someone asks what the population average of an infinite population means,
say that is exactly Lecture 1.2's first frame and leave it.
:::

## Mean, Median and Mode

Three answers to where a distribution sits. They agree only when it is
symmetric:

- **Mean:** the balance point, and the one a long tail pulls.
- **Med\underline{i}an:** the m\textbf{\underline{i}}ddle value, with half the people either side.
- **M\underline{o}de:** the m\textbf{\underline{o}}st common value, at the peak.

The letters tell median and mode apart. The \textbf{\underline{i}} is for
m\textbf{\underline{i}}ddle, the \textbf{\underline{o}} for
m\textbf{\underline{o}}st common.

::: {.defn title="Earnings Push the Mean Above the Median"}
A town's earnings: the median is 26,000 and the mean 34,000. The peak sits
lower still. Report the mean and you describe a person who may not exist.
:::

::: {.notes}
Define the median and the mode properly, because this is the only frame that
does. The median: sort everybody by earnings and take the person in the middle,
so half earn less and half earn more. The mode: the value that turns up most
often, which on a density is the highest point of the curve.

The slide states the trick and marks the letters, so read it off rather than
explaining it. Median and mode are the pair that get swapped in exams; mean is
never confused with either. Those are the only two of the three
words carrying an i and an o, so the hook is exact. Do not extend it to "a for
average", because median has an a in it too and the trick stops working. Mean
is the leftover anyway, and it is the only one of the three you compute rather
than locate - which is also why a billionaire walking into the room moves the
mean and leaves the median where it was.

The newspaper is the example to use. One line for what a town earns, mean
34,000 and median 26,000: ask which one they would print. One number cannot
carry a skewed distribution and an honest headline reports both. This was its
own question frame until 17 September, cut because the module never returns to
the median and the question did not earn the room time.

This is not a technicality about summary statistics. It is the reason a
government can put out a true sentence about average incomes in a year when the
typical household lost ground, and neither number is a lie.

The strict ordering - mode below median below mean - is the usual rule of thumb
for a unimodal right-skewed distribution and it does have counterexamples, so
the frame says "the peak sits lower still" about earnings rather than stating a
law. Do not upgrade it to one.
:::


::: {.tablenotes title="A Symmetric Distribution Has One Centre"}
Navy marks the mode, blue the median, green the mean. On a symmetric
distribution all three sit at the same point.

::: {.notes}
Work the left panel first and get the order out of them before you say it:
the peak is the mode, the middle person is the median, and the mean is dragged
towards the tail. Then the right panel, which is the whole point of showing two
- take the tail away and the three questions have the same answer, which is why
nobody distinguishes them until a distribution is skewed.

Earnings are the left panel. Every wage distribution anybody has measured looks
like this, which is why the median is the number reported for household income
and the mean is the number reported when somebody wants a bigger figure.
:::

## The Variance: Average Squared Distance From the Mean

A mean tells you nothing about whether people cluster near it or scatter. The
variance measures how far a typical person sits from the mean:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
s_x^2 = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( x_i - \bar{x} \right)^2
\end{equation}
```

- $s_x^2$: the variance of $x$ in the sample
- $\sigma_x^2$: the variance of $x$ in the population

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge B-3e, p.695: Var(X) = E[(X - mu)^2], and the squaring is
     there to drop the sign and to treat distances above and below mu
     alike. B-3f, p.696: the standard deviation is the POSITIVE square
     root, sd(X) = +sqrt(Var(X)) - the word positive is in the source and
     is now in the notation line. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Two choices sit inside the formula, and say both out loud. Squaring drops the
sign, so someone five euro below the mean counts as far out as someone five
above. Averaging makes the number comparable across samples of different size.

Squared, not absolute, because the square is what the algebra can carry
through an expectation. Say that and move on: nobody is going to miss the
absolute deviation.

The variance itself is in squared euro, so "how far a typical person sits" is
the picture rather than the arithmetic. The next frame pays that back by
quoting the standard deviation instead.
:::

## Bessel's Correction

An average weights the sum by $1/n$. Bessel's correction weights it by
$1/(n-1)$ instead. Deviations from the sample mean sum to zero, so only $n-1$
are free. The weight moves sharply in small samples:

- **$n = 120$:** $1/119$ against $1/120$, a difference under one per cent.
- **$n = 2$:** the weight is $1$, so the sum of squares is the estimate.
- **$n = 1$:** the weight is $1/0$, so there is no estimate at all.

::: {.notes}
The appendix derivation of Bessel's correction is this week's homework, and problem set 1
opens with it.

Show the forcing on the board in thirty seconds, because the whole frame rests
on it. Put three numbers up, compute their mean, then the three deviations.
Cover the third and ask the room for it. They can always tell you, because the
three have to sum to zero - so the third was never a separate measurement. Two
free deviations out of three, and n-1 out of n.

Read the three weights down the slide rather than explaining them, because the
arithmetic is the argument. At 120 the correction is a rounding error and you
should say so - they will otherwise think they have found a trick worth
arguing about. At 2 the weight is one, so the estimator has stopped averaging
altogether and simply hands back the sum. At 1 it asks for a division by zero
and there is no answer, which is correct: one person carries no information
about how spread out anybody else is.

The n = 2 row is the one to slow down on. A student who notices that the
correction doubles the answer there has spotted something real and should be
told so. It doubles because half the samples of two are two people who happen
to match, and those report a world with no variation in it. The rows that do
show spread are inflated to pay for the rows that show none.

If there is time, enumerate it. Population of two people worth 0 and 2, so the
true variance is 1. The four samples of two give sums of squared deviations 0,
2, 2, 0. Weighted by 1/n those average to 0.5, exactly half the truth. Weighted
by 1/(n-1) they average to 1, exactly right. No expectations taken and the
result is in front of them.

Then say the general rule, because it comes back twice: subtract one from the
denominator for every quantity you estimated from the same data. Lecture 2.3
estimates two and divides by n-2; Lecture 3.1 estimates k+1 and divides by
n-k-1. It is the same sentence every time.

The other half of the story, if a student pushes: the sample mean is also the
number that makes the squared deviations smallest, so deviations from the bar
understate deviations from mu. That is what the appendix derivation turns into
arithmetic. Ben Lambert has two short videos on exactly this, "Estimating the
population variance from a sample", parts one and two, and the first is
entirely intuition - worth pointing at, because this is the frame students
most often say they nodded through.

The derivation is three steps and the last one is the only one that bites: the
gap between the bar and mu has a variance of its own, sigma-squared over n, and
n of those account for exactly one of the n terms.
:::

## The Standard Deviation

The variance is in squared euro, and nothing is measured in those. Taking the
positive square root puts the spread back in euro:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
s_x = \sqrt{s_x^2}
\end{equation}
```

- $s_x$: the standard deviation of $x$ in the sample
- $\sigma_x$: the standard deviation of $x$ in the population

::: {.takeaway title="Read It Against the Mean"}
Our 120 average 12.25 an hour, with a standard deviation of 5.91. Double
everybody's earnings and both numbers double; the variance quadruples.
:::

```{=html}

     root of the variance, and Property SD.2 is sd(aX + b) = |a| sd(X).
     SD.2 is the callout's second sentence and is the real reason the
     standard deviation is the one quoted: it scales with the data, while
     VAR.2, sd's counterpart for the variance, scales with a^2.

     Added 17 September, Sam: the deck defined the standard deviation in a
     notation line on the variance frame and gave its motivation in one
     trailing sentence on the Bessel frame, which was about something else.
     Both moved here. The notation lines for s_x and sigma_x moved off the
     variance frame too, so each symbol is now listed on the frame that
     teaches it, and sigma_x is still introduced before the skewness frame

     THE NUMBERS are the module's own standing sample: mean earnings 12.25
     an hour and standard deviation 5.91, so the variance is about 34.9
     squared euro an hour - the quantity nobody can interpret. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Say "squared euro an hour" out loud rather than hiding behind the word "units".
It is the honest reason the standard deviation is quoted and the variance is
not, and a room that hears it once stops asking why there are two numbers for
one idea.

Put 5.91 next to 12.25 and say what the pair means: a typical person in our
sample sits about six euro an hour away from the average. That sentence is
impossible with the variance, because 34.9 squared euro an hour corresponds to
nothing anybody has ever been paid.

If someone asks why we keep the variance at all, the answer is Lecture 1.2:
variances add and standard deviations do not. The variance of a sum is the sum
of the variances plus twice the covariance, and there is no matching rule for
standard deviations. So the variance is the one the algebra runs on and the
standard deviation is the one you report.
:::

## The Moments of a Distribution

Mean, variance, skewness and kurtosis are the first four moments of a
distribution. The mean locates it; the rest are one bracket at three powers:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
E\left[\left( x - \mu_x \right)^{k}\right], \qquad k = 2,\, 3,\, 4
\end{equation}
```

- $k$: the power, giving the variance, then skewness, then kurtosis

::: {.defn title="A Higher Power Weights the Tails More"}
Double a person's distance from the mean. At $k = 2$ they count four times
more; at $k = 4$, sixteen. Kurtosis is decided by its outliers. An odd power
keeps the sign, so $k = 3$ says which tail is longer.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- The three summaries are one construction at three powers. Wooldridge
     B-3e p.695 and B-3h p.697 give the definitions but not the reason the
     exponent is what it is, so this frame is the module's own exposition
     rather than a claim traced to the shelf. The two facts it rests on are
     arithmetic: an odd power preserves sign, and a higher power weights a
     far deviation more heavily RELATIVE TO a nearer one.

     THE RATIO IS THE POINT, Sam's framing 17 September, and the callout now
     states it with a number rather than talking about cancellation. Double
     a deviation d to 2d: at k = 2 the contribution goes from d^2 to 4d^2, a
     factor of four; at k = 4 it goes from d^4 to 16d^4, a factor of
     sixteen. So the fourth power is decided almost entirely by whatever
     sits furthest out, which IS kurtosis. The old second sentence said only
     that an even power stops deviations cancelling - true, but that is the
     reason kurtosis is positive, not the reason it measures tails.

     Sam's framing, 17 September: use the mathematics itself to give the
     intuition rather than describing each moment separately. This frame is
     that idea, and it is why the skewness and kurtosis frames that follow
     need no formula of their own. Confirmed by Sam later the same day: the
     mechanics stay on distance from the mean and the power, and no per-
     moment equation goes on any slide.

     THE TERM IS NOW TAUGHT, also Sam's instruction. The frame is titled
     after it, the lead names all four as the first four moments, and the k
     line maps the power to the named statistic. Correction (b) in the
     header, which removed moment-numbering from the skewness notes to
     avoid a raw/central/standardised mismatch, was the wrong remedy: the
     answer is to use the term correctly, not to avoid it. The exact
     bookkeeping - first moment about zero, second about the mean, third and
     fourth standardised by sigma^3 and sigma^4 - is now in the notes for
     the lecturer and is deliberately not on the slide. Wooldridge B-3h,
     p.697, is the locator for the standardised definitions. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Two minutes, and it pays for both of the next two frames. Say "moments" out
loud and say it is the standard word, because they will meet it in every
statistics course and in every textbook treatment of this material. The slide
now names all four; what it does not carry is the exact bookkeeping, and that
is what you add here if anyone asks.

The bookkeeping, for you rather than for them. The mean is the first moment
taken about zero. The variance is the second moment taken about the mean, which
is what "central" means. Skewness and kurtosis are the third and fourth central
moments divided by sigma cubed and sigma to the fourth, and that division is
what makes them unit-free and comparable across distributions. So "the first
four moments" mixes one raw moment, one central moment and two standardised
ones. That is the standard informal usage, it is what every other source will
say to them, and the frame says it too - but do not let a sharp student catch
you out on the detail.

Make the recurrence explicit, because it is the reason this frame exists rather
than three separate definitions. Point at the bracket and say: you have already
met this at the second power, it is the variance. The third and the fourth are
the next twenty minutes. Lecture 1.2 writes the variance and the covariance as
expectations of exactly this shape, and the standard error in 1.3 and the
variance of the slope in 2.3 are both built from it. A student who reads the
bracket as a template stops memorising formulas; a student who reads each one as
new has four things to learn instead of one.

Say what the family buys, too: a distribution is not one number, and the moments
are the ordered set of numbers that describe its structure - where it sits, how
wide it is, which way it leans, how much lives out in the tails.

Put three deviations
on the board, say plus two, minus two and plus four euro, and run them through
each power. The four euro is twice the distance of the twos, so watch what that
doubling is worth at each power. At the second power the twos give four and the
four gives sixteen: four times as much. At the third power the minus two gives minus
eight and the sign survives, which is the whole of skewness. At the fourth power the twos give sixteen
and the four gives 256: sixteen times as much, so the answer is decided almost
entirely by the one person out in the tail, which is the whole of kurtosis.

That ratio is the mechanism and it is worth saying in one line: the further out
somebody sits, the more a higher power favours them, and kurtosis is the power
that favours them most.

Say explicitly that this is one construction, not three. A student who sees
that does not have to memorise three formulas. The scaling by the standard
deviation on the third and fourth is what makes them unit-free and comparable
across distributions; that is the same move as correlation on covariance in
the next section, and it is worth naming the repeat.
:::

## Skewness

Skewness asks which side of the mean has the longer tail. Cube the deviations,
then divide by $\sigma_x^3$ to strip the units:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\text{skew}(x) = \frac{E\left[\left( x - \mu_x \right)^{3}\right]}{\sigma_x^{3}}
\end{equation}
```

- **Below 0.5:** approximately symmetric.
- **0.5 to 1:** moderately skewed.
- **Above 1:** highly skewed.

::: {.caveat title="Bulmer's Bands Read the Size, Not the Sign"}
Positive means a long right tail, negative a long left one [@bulmer1979]. The
bands apply to the number with the sign stripped off.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge B-3h, p.697: skewness is the third moment of the
     standardised variable, E[(X - mu)^3] / sigma^3. Added as its own frame
     17 September, Sam: each moment equation gets a slide of its own, and
     the moments frame keeps only the general form.

     THE CONVERSE DOES NOT HOLD and the frame is worded to avoid claiming
     it: symmetry implies zero skewness, zero skewness does not imply
     symmetry.

     BULMER'S BANDS, added 18 September at Sam's request, on the Cohen
     pattern used for correlation: below 0.5 approximately symmetric, 0.5
     to 1 moderately skewed, above 1 highly skewed. Bulmer, Principles of
     Statistics, 1979 Dover reprint of the 1965 second edition, is the
     source everyone attributes these to, and bulmer1979 is now in the bib.
     NOT on this module's shelf - Wooldridge B-3h gives the definition and
     no interpretation at all, exactly as with the correlation. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Cube on the board with two numbers and it lands in ten seconds: plus two cubes
to plus eight, minus two to minus eight. The signs survive, so the sum tells
you which side won. Squaring would have thrown that away, which is exactly why
the variance says nothing about shape.

Dividing by sigma cubed is the same move as correlation on covariance, one
section later: strip the units so two distributions can be compared. Name the
repeat when you get there.
:::

## Skewness: Which Tail Runs Longer

```{=latex}
\figpair{../_shared/figures/1-1_skew-negative.png}{Negative skew: the long
tail runs left.}{../_shared/figures/1-1_skew-positive.png}{Positive skew: the
long tail runs right.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="The Tail Pulls the Mean"}
This is the third power: both curves share the mean and the variance. Grey marks the
median, green the mean, which sits out in the tail.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge B-3h, p.697: skewness is the third moment of the
     standardised variable, E[(X - mu)^3] / sigma^3, and a symmetric
     distribution makes it zero. The deck states no formula, so there is no
     normalisation to get wrong; the appendix is where it would go if a
     cohort asks.

     CORRECTED. The notes used to say "the first two moments cannot tell
     them apart". B-3h numbers skewness and kurtosis as the third and fourth
     moments of the STANDARDISED variable, and never numbers the variance,
     so naming the mean and the variable's variance directly avoids a
     mismatch that bought nothing.

     NOT IN THE SOURCE. That the mean is pulled into the long tail is a
     description of these exhibits, which our builder draws, and it is the
     standard teaching claim. Wooldridge B-3c, p.694, gives only the
     converse: a distribution symmetric about m has m as both mean and
     median. Left as drafted and flagged, not hedged. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Walk it: both panels have identical mean and identical variance, so the two
numbers the room has learned so far are useless here. What separates them is
which side the long tail is on.

The median is the value with half the area either side of it, so a long tail
adds area far out without moving the halfway point. The mean has to balance
that area, so it follows the tail.
:::

## Kurtosis

Kurtosis asks how much of the distribution sits far from the mean. Raise the
deviations to the fourth power, then divide by $\sigma_x^4$:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\text{kurt}(x) = \frac{E\left[\left( x - \mu_x \right)^{4}\right]}{\sigma_x^{4}}
\end{equation}
```

- **Below 3:** thinner tails than the normal curve.
- **Exactly 3:** the normal curve itself.
- **Above 3:** thicker tails, and more weight in them.

::: {.caveat title="No Agreed Bands, Only the Benchmark"}
Nobody has settled bands for kurtosis the way Bulmer did for skewness. Daily
stock returns sit well above three. Finance cares about kurtosis for that
reason.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge B-3h, p.697: kurtosis is the fourth moment of the
     standardised variable, E[(X - mu)^4] / sigma^4, and larger values mean
     thicker tails. Added as its own frame 17 September, Sam.

     NO BANDS EXIST FOR KURTOSIS and the frame says so rather than
     inventing some. Bulmer has bands for skewness and no counterpart for
     kurtosis; the only agreed reference point is the normal curve's 3, and
     the vocabulary built on it - platykurtic below, mesokurtic at,
     leptokurtic above - which the deck does not use because the words cost
     more than they buy in a first course. The finance anchor is the honest
     way to make 3 mean something: fat-tailed daily returns are the standard
     case and the reason the benchmark is worth knowing.

     THE BENCHMARK OF THREE IS NOT IN WOOLDRIDGE. B-3h gives no reference
     value and the source carries no excess-kurtosis convention, so the deck
     does not subtract three anywhere. The value 3 for the normal is
     standard and correct, and it is stated here because "larger means
     thicker" is uninterpretable without something to be larger than. Flag
     if you would rather it came off the slide. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Three is the number to make them write down, because kurtosis is meaningless
without it. Everything is measured against the normal curve: at three the tails
are normal, above three they are thicker, below three thinner.

Say plainly that this is the least useful of the four for this module and that
it earns its place because finance runs on it. Returns are the standard case of
tails far heavier than a normal curve would allow, and a risk model built on
the normal understates how often a very bad day happens.
:::

## Kurtosis: How Much Sits Far From the Middle

```{=latex}
\figpair{../_shared/figures/1-1_kurtosis-light.png}{Light tails: almost
nothing lands far out.}{../_shared/figures/1-1_kurtosis-heavy.png}{Heavy
tails: much more lands a long way out.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="Thicker Tails, Same Variance"}
This is the fourth power: both panels share the normal curve's mean and variance. What
changes is how often a value turns up far out.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- CORRECTED. The right-hand caption read "a sharper peak, and far more in
     the tails". Wooldridge B-3h, p.697, defines kurtosis as the fourth
     moment of the standardised variable, E[(X - mu)^4] / sigma^4, and says
     only this about interpreting it: "larger values mean that the tails in
     the distribution of X are thicker". The peak is not in the source, so
     the caption now claims the tails alone.

     Note also what the source does NOT do: it states no excess-kurtosis
     convention, never subtracts three, and says outright that without a
     reference value the level of E[Z^4] is hard to interpret. The value
     for the normal is obtained in B-5. This deck therefore states no
     number and no normalisation. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Both panels have the same mean and the same variance, again, so again the first
two summaries are blind to the difference. What changes is how often something
lands a long way out.

Financial returns look like the second panel, which is why models built on the
first underestimate how often a crash happens. Said out loud only: there is no
source for it on this module's shelf.
:::

## The Range

The range is the measure everybody reaches for first. It is also the only one
here that is not a moment:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\text{range} = x_{\max} - x_{\min}
\end{equation}
```

::: {.caveat title="Two People Decide the Range"}
Every other observation could move without changing it. A bigger sample can
only widen the range, never narrow it.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Added 17 September, Sam: the deck had no range at all.

     MOVED the same day, also Sam, from before the variance to the end of
     the section. The range is not a moment - it is a difference of two
     order statistics, not an average of deviations - so placing it inside
     the run-up to the moments family cut across the one construction the
     section is built on. It reads better as the coda: finish the family,
     then show the measure that sits outside it and say why. The variance
     never needed the range to motivate it anyway; its own frame is
     motivated by the mean saying nothing about scatter.

     NOT FROM THE SHELF. Wooldridge's Math Refresher B has no range; B-3e
     p.695 starts at the variance. Both claims in the callout are
     arithmetic: the range depends only on the two extreme order
     statistics, and a superset of a sample cannot have a smaller max or a
     larger min, so the range is non-decreasing in n. -->
```

::: {.notes}
This frame is at the end on purpose, and the set-up for it happens twenty
minutes earlier. When you open the spread material, ask the room for a measure
of spread; somebody will say the range. Take it, write it on the board, and
leave it there unanswered until now.

Then break it, with the moments fresh. Move every observation except the top
and the bottom one: the range does not move. Then the worse property - draw
more people and the range can only grow, so two samples of different size
cannot be compared on it at all. Nothing in the moments family has either
problem, because every one of them uses all n observations rather than two.
:::


# Describing Two Variables

## Covariance: Measuring How Two Variables Move Together

Each variable has its own mean. Every person has a distance from each, and the
covariance multiplies the two:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
s_{xy} = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n}
         \left( x_i - \bar{x} \right)\left( y_i - \bar{y} \right)
\end{equation}
```

- $s_{xy}$: the covariance of $x$ and $y$ in the sample

::: {.defn title="Same Side Positive, Opposite Sides Negative"}
Above on both, or below on both, and the product is positive. Above on one and
below on the other, and it is negative.
:::

## The Sign Is the Part You Can Read

Sum those products across all 120 people, and ours comes out positive:

- **Positive:** above-average schooling mostly comes with above-average earnings.
- **Negative:** above-average schooling mostly comes with below-average earnings.
- **Near Zero:** the products cancel, so no straight-line relationship shows.

::: {.takeaway title="Zero Is Cancellation, Not a Convention"}
Zero does not mean unrelated by definition. It means the positive products and
the negative ones came out even.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Split from the covariance frame, 17 September. The old frame did the
     mechanics - multiply the signs, add them up - and stopped there, so it
     said how the number is BUILT and never what it TELLS you. That second
     half is this frame.

     WOOLDRIDGE B-4b, p.698 is the middle bullet and it is a fact-check
     correction that must survive: "If sigma_XY < 0, then, on average, when
     X is above its mean, Y is below its mean." Do not weaken "mostly" to a
     bare negation.

     ZERO IS THE POINT OF THE FRAME. A first course states that zero
     covariance means no linear relationship as though it were a definition.
     It is not - it is what cancellation looks like when the agreements and
     the disagreements are evenly matched. A student who has that does not
     need to memorise the zero case.

     ORDER MATTERS. This frame says the SIGN is readable; the frame after it
     says the SIZE is not. Do not add a magnitude claim here ("and by how
     much"), because the next frame spends itself contradicting it. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Two minutes, and say the mechanism twice because it is the whole frame. Each
variable is measured against its own mean. Every person therefore has two
distances, and the covariance is the average of their products.

Add the half the slide has no room for: the products are not the same size.
Someone a year above average on schooling and fifty cents above on earnings
contributes almost nothing. Someone four years above and fifteen euro above
contributes sixty, because the product multiplies both distances. That is why
the formula multiplies the deviations rather than just counting the signs - and
it is also why one extreme person can carry a covariance, which is the outlier
problem Lecture 2.1 meets properly.

Push on the zero case if there is time. Ask what a cloud with zero covariance
looks like: not an empty scatter, but one where for every person above on both
there is another above on one and below on the other. The cancelling is
visible in the picture, and that is worth more than the sentence.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- IDEA 3. 81-92 min.

     Wooldridge B-4b, p.697: Cov(X, Y) = E[(X - mu_X)(Y - mu_Y)], built
     from exactly this product of deviations, and his own set-up runs
     through the four sign cases the frame's notes use.

     ORDER FIXED 18 September, Sam: the equation leads and the two sign
     cases moved into a callout. They had been bullets sitting ABOVE the
     equation, which is the one place the skill's equation pattern does not
     put anything - a plain sentence introduces the equation, the notation
     list follows it, and an argument about a symbol is a separate callout.

     LEAD REWRITTEN 17 September, Sam's framing: covariance works because
     each variable is measured against ITS OWN mean and the two distances
     are multiplied. The lead had used a voting metaphor - every person
     casts a vote, the covariance is the tally - which described the sign
     behaviour without ever stating the mechanism, and was the same
     borrowed-metaphor fault as "The Gap Eats One Term". Votes are gone from
     both covariance frames and from the notes.

     CORRECTED in the notes on the next frame: it said the n-1 was there
     because "two sample means have been used up", which predicts n-2 and
     is wrong. The sample covariance weights by 1/(n-1) because
     E[sum (x_i - xbar)(y_i - ybar)] = (n-1) sigma_xy, the cross-product
     term being n Cov(xbar, ybar) = sigma_xy. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Put the four cases on the board rather than reading the slide: above and above,
below and below, above and below, below and above. The slide states the sign;
the board is where the room sees the sum count the positives against the
negatives.

A single person contributes nothing when they sit exactly at one of the two
means, which is worth saying if someone asks what the zero case looks like.

The weight is Bessel's correction again. Someone will expect 1/(n-2) here,
since two means were estimated rather than one; it is 1/(n-1), because the
expected sum of cross-products comes to (n-1) sigma_xy. The free-deviations
shortcut does not transfer cleanly to two variables, so do not wave at it -
say that the algebra gives n-1 and that the appendix for it is Lecture 1.2.
:::

## Why the Size of a Covariance Is Not Interpretable

The same 120 people and the same relationship, measured three ways:

- **Earnings in Euro an Hour:** 8.11 euro-years
- **Earnings in Cents an Hour:** 811.16 cent-years
- **Schooling in Months Instead:** 97.34 euro-months

::: {.takeaway title="Only the Yardstick Changed"}
Nothing about these 120 people changed from one line to the next. Only the
units did, so the size of a covariance carries no information.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- CORRECTED, then MOVED. The frame used to say a negative covariance
     "says they do not" rise together, which is a bare negation and weaker
     than the source. Wooldridge B-4b, p.698: "If sigma_XY < 0, then, on
     average, when X is above its mean, Y is below its mean." That
     corrected sentence now lives on the covariance frame, which is the one
     about the sign; this frame is only about the size. The correction is
     NOT dropped - do not reinstate it here.

     THE THREE NUMBERS, 17 September. Computed from the module's own
     C_02_05_sample_df, n = 120, not invented: cov in euro-years 8.11, in
     cent-years 811.16, with schooling in months 97.34, and the correlation
     0.594 in every case (8.11 / (2.31 x 5.91) = 0.594). Recompute if
     B_03 changes.

     The scaling claim is Property Cov.2, p.698:
     Cov(a1 X + b1, a2 Y + b2) = a1 a2 Cov(X, Y). Euro to cents is
     a2 = 100 with a1 = 1, so the covariance multiplies by a hundred
     exactly. -->
```

::: {.notes}
"On average" is doing real work in both sentences: a positive covariance does
not mean every high-schooling person out-earns every low-schooling one, only
that the positive products outweigh the negative ones.

Nothing about the world has changed when you switch to cents, which is the
whole complaint.
:::

## Correlation Is Covariance With the Units Divided Out

The covariance carries euro-years; so does the product of the two standard
deviations. Divide and the units cancel:

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
r_{xy} = \frac{s_{xy}}{s_x \, s_y}
\end{equation}
```

- $r_{xy}$: the correlation of $x$ and $y$ in the sample

::: {.takeaway title="All Three Become 0.594"}
Every one of those three covariances divides down to 0.594. Both standard
deviations are positive, so the covariance's sign survives.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge B-4c, p.699, equation B.29:
     Corr(X, Y) = Cov(X, Y) / (sd(X) sd(Y)) = sigma_XY / (sigma_X sigma_Y),
     "sometimes denoted rho_XY", which is the Greek symbol on this frame. -->
```

::: {.notes}
The denominator is a product of two standard deviations, so it carries
euro-years as well, and the ratio is a pure number. That is the entire trick.
:::

## Correlation Runs From Minus One to One

Correlation says how strong the relationship is, not only which way it runs.
Price and quantity demanded move opposite ways, so that correlation is negative.

::: {.takeaway title="One Means an Exact Line"}
At $1$ or $-1$ the points lie exactly on a straight line. Values nearer either
end mean a stronger straight-line relationship. Measure earnings in cents and
nothing moves.
:::

```{=html}
<!-- Wooldridge B-4c, pp.698-699. "Because sigma_X and sigma_Y are
     positive, Cov(X, Y) and Corr(X, Y) always have the same sign."
     Property Corr.1: -1 <= Corr(X, Y) <= 1. Corr(X, Y) = 1 implies
     Y = a + bX with b > 0, and -1 the same with b < 0; "values of rho_XY
     closer to 1 or -1 indicate stronger linear relationships". Property
     Corr.2 gives the invariance, for a1 a2 > 0 - and euro to cents is
     a2 = 100 > 0, so the sign condition holds here. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Wooldridge says the extreme cases of plus or minus one rarely occur, and he is
right: a correlation of exactly one in real data usually means the same
variable has been entered twice.

Note the asymmetry worth carrying: independence implies zero correlation, but
zero correlation does not imply independence. Wooldridge gives the standard
counterexample, a variable and its own square. Lecture 3.1 needs that distinction.
:::

## Small, Medium and Large: 0.1, 0.3, 0.5

Cohen's conventions, the ones you will meet everywhere [@cohen1988]:

- **$r = 0.1$:** small.
- **$r = 0.3$:** medium.
- **$r = 0.5$:** large.

::: {.caveat title="Cohen Wrote These for Psychology"}
Wooldridge gives no bands at all. Ours is 0.594, large by Cohen. Squared, it
says the two share a third of their variation.
:::

```{=latex}

{../_shared/figures/1-1_cohen-medium.png}{Cohen's medium.}%
{../_shared/figures/1-1_cohen-strong.png}{Cohen's large.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="Earnings Depend on More Than Schooling"}
Even the panel Cohen calls large is a wide cloud. Earnings depend on far more
than schooling, which is what block 3 adds.
:::


::: {.notes}
Somebody will ask whether adding more variables tightens the cloud, and the
honest answer needs care. Adding a variable does not make a CORRELATION
clearer - a correlation is a two-variable object and does not change when a
third arrives. What multiple regression does is account for some of the other
things earnings depend on, so that what is left over is smaller. Do not say
"the fit improves as you add variables": R-squared rises when you add any
variable at all, including a useless one, which is Lecture 2.2's warning, and
Lecture 3.1 is a whole frame on controls that make the estimate worse. The
sentence that survives all of that is the one in the box: the cloud is wide
because schooling is not the whole story, and block 3 is where the rest of the
story goes.

Put this up straight after the bands and say nothing for a few seconds. The
room expects "large" to look like a line and it does not - at 0.5 the cloud is
still wide enough that knowing schooling tells you very little about any one
person's earnings. That gap between the word and the picture is the honest
content of the previous frame, and it is worth more than the numbers.

The panels share the same 160 people on the horizontal axis, so what changes
across the three is only how tightly earnings track schooling.
:::


::: {.notes}
This is the rule of thumb worth carrying out of the lecture, because it is the
one that deflates the number correctly. A correlation of 0.6 sounds like most
of the story and is about a third of it.

Do the working example out loud: our schooling and earnings correlation is
0.594, so a shade over a third of the variation in earnings moves with
schooling and the rest does not. Then remind them what we already know about
this population - the return is a real 1.30 an hour, we wrote it ourselves -
so a third is what a genuine, exactly known effect looks like in a correlation.
That pairing is the whole lesson.

On the bands: do not tell the room they are wrong, tell them where they come
from. In labour economics a
cross-sectional correlation of 0.6 between two things measured on individuals
is about as strong as it gets, and a "weak" 0.2 can carry an effect worth
billions. Strength and importance are different questions, which is the point
the application frame closes on.

This frame is also the first appearance of the squaring move that becomes
R-squared in 2.2. Say so, so that frame arrives as a return rather than a new
idea.
:::

## Correlation Measures Straight-Line Association Only

```{=latex}
\fig{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Four samples from this population, each with a correlation of 0.60.}
```

::: {.tablenotes title="Same Number, Four Clouds"}
A curve, four outliers and two separate groups all return 0.60. One statistic
cannot tell them apart [@anscombe1973graphs; @matejka2017].
:::


::: {.notes}
Walk the four panels in order: the honest one, the curve that turns over, the
flat cloud that four points drag into a slope, and the two clusters with no
relationship inside either. Then say all four correlations are 0.60.

Four different worlds, four different answers to what schooling is worth, and
one summary statistic that cannot separate them. The lesson is old and keeps
needing to be relearned, which is why there are two citations forty-four years
apart.
:::

## Why a Correlation Is Not a Causal Claim

Schooling really does raise earnings here by 1.30 an hour a year. We wrote the
generator that way. Outside a simulation you are handed the correlation and not
the generator.

::: {.caveat title="0.594 Is Consistent With No Effect"}
The same 0.594 could come from a world where schooling changes nothing. The
number alone cannot tell you which world you are in.
:::

## Three Ways a Correlation Misleads

All three are real correlations, and each one goes wrong differently:

- **Coincidence:** films starring Nicolas Cage track pool drownings, $r = 0.66$.
- **A Common Cause:** on sunny days people buy ice cream, and people swim.
- **A Difference That Pays:** people who stay in school longer differ in more than schooling.

::: {.caveat title="Ice Cream Does Not Cause Drowning"}
Nothing connects Cage to drownings at all. Sunshine drives both the ice cream
and the swimming. Ability raises schooling and earnings alike. The correlation
looks identical in all three.
:::

```{=html}

     the part that transfers.

     and two across this frame and the one before it, so the seam read as
     arbitrary and the ability objection looked like a separate point rather
     than the third member of a list. Ability moved onto this frame as the
     third bullet. The frame before now carries the reveal instead: that the
     same 0.594 is consistent with a true effect of zero.

     THE THREE CASES ARE DIFFERENT and the frame exists to separate them.
     Cage and drownings is COINCIDENCE - no mechanism of any kind, found by
     dredging thousands of series until two lined up. Ice cream and drowning
     is CONFOUNDING by a common cause, both genuinely caused by summer.
     Schooling and earnings is CONFOUNDING by a difference that pays, which
     is the one this module spends a term on. A student who thinks
     "correlation is not causation" means only the second has not understood
     the first.

     LOCATOR. The Cage pairing is Tyler Vigen's, @vigen2015, and r = 0.66 is
     as stated in the LibreTexts introductory statistics text (Geraghty,
     3.6.03 "Correlation vs. Causation"), which also draws the coincidence
     against confounding distinction this frame uses. Vigen is NOT on the
     shelf - the example is described and attributed here, not reproduced.

     FORWARD LINKS. The dredging point is 3.3's specification search: hunt
     across enough pairs and correlations like this appear by construction.
     The common-cause point is 3.1's confounder. Both are named in the

```

::: {.notes}
The Cage example gets a laugh and then it has to earn its place, so follow it
with the question: how did anyone find that? Vigen ran a search across
thousands of public series looking for pairs that moved together. At that scale
correlations like this are not a surprise, they are arithmetic - which is
exactly the argument Lecture 3.3 makes about searching across specifications
until something comes out significant.

Draw the difference on the board, because it is the whole frame. Cage to
drownings: no arrow anywhere, the two series have nothing to do with each
other. Ice cream to drownings: sunshine at the top with two arrows coming down
out of it, one to ice cream and one to swimming, and swimming on to drowning.
Then rub out nothing and ask the room to find the arrow from ice cream to
drowning. There isn't one, and that is the point - the two things we measured
are cousins, not parent and child.

Say the denial out loud rather than leaving it implied: ice cream does not
cause drowning. A student who only hears "they are correlated because of the
weather" has been given the mechanism and not the conclusion.

The third bullet is the one the module lives on, so slow down for it. Ability,
family money and stamina all raise schooling and raise earnings, and none of
them is in the data. Lecture 3.1 gives that a name and an arithmetic for which
way it throws the estimate.

Resist giving the fourth kind here. Reverse causation is 4.2 and the room has
enough.
:::

::: {.notes}
Today it is enough that you can say the sentence. Lecture 3.1 turns it into omitted
variable bias and gives you the formula for which way the estimate is thrown.

If a student asks for the real number: Mincer's census regressions give about
seven per cent a year without controls and about eleven with experience
controls. Neither is a causal effect and Mastering 'Metrics 6.1 says so.
:::

## What Would Have To Be True Today?

Today's number is the correlation between schooling and earnings in our sample.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

```{=html}
<!-- 97-102 min. The standing question, run for the first time. The wording
     in the box is Sam's and matches the announcement frame in section one
     word for word; it is not trimmed.

     THIS FRAME ABSORBED A SECOND QUESTION, cut 17 September: "Two Studies,
     One Correlation of 0.42", which sat five minutes earlier and asked
     whether two studies reporting the same number had found the same thing.
     It asked what this frame asks, and section three was carrying three
     interaction points in fifteen consecutive minutes on eleven minutes of
     content. Section three now runs 81-97 instead of 81-92. The list the
     room builds is preserved in the notes below. -->
```

::: {.notes}
They will struggle to say what they would need to see, and the list they build
getting there - the scatterplot, the sample size, who was left out, what else
differs between two studies - is the syllabus for the rest of the term. Write
it up and leave it up.

Candidate answer for this week, after the room has had a go: a correlation
means what we said it means only if the cloud it summarises is a straight line,
and only if the sample it came from stands in for the population. Neither is
checkable from the number itself.

The point is not that causation is hard in the abstract. It is that THIS
estimate rests on two nameable conditions, and both of them may well be false.
:::

## Application: The Four Numbers on Our Sample

Open the sample of 120 and plot the cloud. Compute the mean, median, standard
deviation, and the correlation of schooling with earnings.

::: {.defn title="Question"}
We built this population so a year of schooling is worth 1.30. Does that make
the correlation close to one?
:::


```{=html}
<!-- 102-107 min. Answers BEFORE the computation, which is the surviving
     form of predict-before-reveal in this module: no hands, no revote,
     just a number on the board that the run either matches or does not. -->
```

::: {.notes}
The answer is no, and the reason is the whole of section three. Correlation
measures how tightly the cloud hugs the line, not how steep the line is. The
effect here is real, it is exact, and we wrote it down ourselves - and the
correlation still comes nowhere near one, because earnings vary for a hundred
reasons that have nothing to do with schooling.

That is the sentence to get out of the room before running anything: a strong
true effect and a modest correlation sit together perfectly happily. Most people
expect the two to travel together and they do not. Lecture 2.2 rebuilds exactly
this argument with the R-squared, so the wrong intuition is worth surfacing here
where it costs nothing.

Lab this week: compute all four by hand from the formulas, then check them
against `mean()`, `median()`, `sd()` and `cor()`. Getting the same answer twice
by two routes is the point, not the answer.
:::

## Three Ways to Describe Data

Today was three separate ideas, each answering a different question:

::: {.contributions}
1. **Populations and Samples.** The question is about a population; the gap to the sample never closes.
2. **Describing One Variable.** Centre, spread and shape each answer one question, and each throws something away.
3. **Describing Two Variables.** Covariance and correlation measure straight-line co-movement, and nothing else.
:::

## Derivation: Bessel's Correction

No other number makes the squared deviations smaller than $\bar{x}$ does. So the
expected sum of squared deviations from $\bar{x}$ comes to $(n-1)\sigma_x^2$,
not $n\sigma_x^2$.

::: {.worked title="The Cross Term Merges Into the Gap"}
Write each deviation from $\bar{x}$ as a deviation from $\mu_x$ minus the gap.
Square and sum, and the cross term merges into the squared gap. Take
expectations of what is left.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]

```{=html}
<!-- CORRECTED. The old wording said the cross term "collapses", which reads
     as "vanishes". It does not. Writing d_i = x_i - mu and g = xbar - mu:

       sum (x_i - xbar)^2 = sum (d_i - g)^2
                          = sum d_i^2 - 2 g sum d_i + n g^2
                          = sum d_i^2 - 2 n g^2 + n g^2
                          = sum d_i^2 - n g^2,

     because sum d_i = n g. So the cross term does not disappear; it doubles
     the squared-gap term and reverses its sign. Taking expectations,
     E[sum d_i^2] = n sigma^2 and E[g^2] = Var(xbar) = sigma^2 / n, so

       E[sum (x_i - xbar)^2] = n sigma^2 - n (sigma^2 / n) = (n-1) sigma^2.

     Wooldridge C-2b, p.716, for the definition of unbiasedness this makes
     the n-1 estimator satisfy. -->
```

::: {.notes}
The step that does the work is the last one, because the gap between $\bar{x}$
and $\mu_x$ has a variance of its own, sigma-squared over n, and n copies of it
eat exactly one term.

Dividing by n instead gives an estimator whose expectation is too small by the
factor (n-1)/n. Any one sample can still come out high; the bias is a property
of the average over samples, not of a draw.
:::

## The Greek Alphabet: Alpha to Mu

Say them out loud. A symbol you cannot pronounce is one you will never ask
about:

| Lower | Upper | Name | Said as | Used here for |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| $\alpha$ | $A$ | alpha | AL-fa | |
| $\beta$ | $B$ | beta | BEE-ta | the regression coefficients, from 2.1 |
| $\gamma$ | $\Gamma$ | gamma | GAM-a | |
| $\delta$ | $\Delta$ | delta | DEL-ta | a shift; $\Delta$ for a change in |
| $\epsilon$ | $E$ | epsilon | EP-si-lon | |
| $\zeta$ | $Z$ | zeta | ZEE-ta | |
| $\eta$ | $H$ | eta | EE-ta | |
| $\theta$ | $\Theta$ | theta | THEE-ta | |
| $\iota$ | $I$ | iota | eye-OH-ta | |
| $\kappa$ | $K$ | kappa | KAP-a | |
| $\lambda$ | $\Lambda$ | lambda | LAM-da | |
| $\mu$ | $M$ | mu | MEW | a population mean |

## The Greek Alphabet: Nu to Omega

| Lower | Upper | Name | Said as | Used here for |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| $\nu$ | $N$ | nu | NEW | |
| $\xi$ | $\Xi$ | xi | KSY | |
| $o$ | $O$ | omicron | OH-mi-kron | |
| $\pi$ | $\Pi$ | pi | PY | |
| $\rho$ | $P$ | rho | ROH | |
| $\sigma$ | $\Sigma$ | sigma | SIG-ma | a population spread; $\Sigma$ means add up |
| $\tau$ | $T$ | tau | TAW | |
| $\upsilon$ | $\Upsilon$ | upsilon | UP-si-lon | |
| $\phi$ | $\Phi$ | phi | FY | |
| $\chi$ | $X$ | chi | KY | |
| $\psi$ | $\Psi$ | psi | SY | |
| $\omega$ | $\Omega$ | omega | OH-mig-a | |

Thirteen capitals are identical to ours, so nobody uses them as symbols.
A capital alpha is just an A.

```{=html}
<!-- Added 17 September, on Sam's request. Appendix, so it is Roman-numbered
     and costs the deck nothing, and .allowframebreaks lets LaTeX split the
     table rather than forcing a two-frame split by hand.

     The "Used here for" column is filled ONLY where the use was verified in
     the repo: beta (49 occurrences across the decks as beta_0, beta_1,
     beta_2, beta_j), delta (7, the dummy shift in 3.2), mu (population
     mean), sigma (population spread) and Sigma (summation). Gamma appears
     ten times but always inside a figure or app expression rather than as a
     named quantity, so it is left blank rather than given an invented
     meaning. Epsilon is blank because this module writes the error as u_i,
     not epsilon_i - worth knowing, because most textbooks use epsilon and a
     student reading around will meet it.

     Pronunciations are the British and Irish ones: beta is BEE-ta, not
     BAY-ta, and zeta is ZEE-ta. Say so if a student has learned the US
     forms, rather than correcting them. -->
```

::: {.notes}
Do not read this out. It is a lookup table, and its whole job is to be there in
week six when someone cannot say sigma and so does not ask.

Point at it once, in week one, and say the thing that actually unblocks people:
nobody is born knowing these, every economist learned them by saying them
wrong in public first, and the cost of not asking is a term of half-read
equations.

The last line is worth thirty seconds. A student who notices that capital
alpha, beta, epsilon and the rest are just Roman capitals has understood
something real about why the notation is the way it is, rather than
memorising a table.
:::

## How to Study This Subject

- **Re-derive:** the week's central result, from a blank page, before the tutorial.
- **Attempt:** the problem set before reading the answers, not after.
- **Space:** the work across the week, since four short days beat one long.
- **Avoid:** rereading and highlighting, which give fluency without retrieval.

::: {.caveat title="Nothing on This Frame Is Examinable"}
Ten minutes today, and no time after that. The four habits above are worth more
than any revision guide.
:::
